entry: 1988 Japanese animated war film written and directed by Isao Takahata. Adapted from Akiyuki Nosaka's 1967 semi-autobiographical short story, *Grave of the Fireflies* follows two orphaned siblings struggling to survive in [[Kobe]] during the final months of the [[Pacific War]]. Animated by [[Studio Ghibli]] and released by [[Toho]] on April 16, 1988, it was a modest box-office success in Japan. Critics have praised its emotional weight, and it has been cited as one of the saddest films ever made. Several critics considered it an anti-war film, but Takahata disagreed.

Loose aggregation of rock fragments. Gravel occurs naturally through sedimentary and erosive geological processes and is also produced commercially as crushed stone. It is classified by particle size: on the Udden-Wentworth scale, granular gravel measures 2–4 mm and pebble gravel 4–64 mm, while ISO 14688 grades gravel as fine, medium or coarse. One cubic metre typically weighs about 1,800 kg. [[Quartz]] is the most common mineral in gravel because it is hard, chemically inert and lacks cleavage planes. Almost half of gravel production is used as [[Concrete|aggregate for concrete]], and much of the rest goes to road construction. Porous gravel deposits have a high hydraulic conductivity, making them important [[Aquifer|aquifers]]. Wind-formed gravel megaripples in [[Argentina]] have been suggested to have counterparts on [[Mars]].

[[Acceleration]] of an object in free fall within a vacuum, caused exclusively by gravitational attraction. In a given gravitational field, all bodies accelerate in a vacuum at the same rate regardless of mass or composition; measuring these rates is called gravimetry. Earth's gravity results from the combined effect of gravitation and the centrifugal force from [[Earth's rotation]] at a fixed point on the surface. Free-fall acceleration on Earth's surface ranges from 9.764 to 9.834 m/s² (32.03 to 32.26 ft/s²), depending on altitude, [[Latitude|latitude]] and [[Longitude|longitude]]. A conventional standard value is defined as exactly 9.80665 m/s². Locations with significant variation from this value are known as gravity anomalies. The figure does not account for effects such as [[Buoyancy|buoyancy]] or [[Drag (physics)|drag]].

Empirical physical constant giving the strength of the gravitational field induced by a mass. Denoted by the capital letter G, it is also called the universal gravitational constant or the Cavendish gravitational constant. It is the proportionality constant in [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|Newton's law]] and a constant term in the Einstein field equations of [[General relativity|general relativity]]. Its value in SI units is approximately 6.6743×10⁻¹¹ m³⋅kg⁻¹⋅s⁻². The first implicit measurement, accurate to within about 1%, is attributed to [[Henry Cavendish]] in a 1798 experiment.

Theoretical condition in which gravity is predicted to be so intense that [[Spacetime|spacetime]] itself would break down. In [[General relativity|general relativity]], a singularity is defined by curvature becoming infinite or by an incomplete geodesic. The theory predicts that any object collapsing beyond its [[Schwarzschild radius]] forms a [[Black hole|black hole]], inside which a singularity forms; an [[Event horizon|event horizon]] covers it. At the start of the [[Big Bang]], the initial state of the universe was predicted to be a singularity of infinite density and temperature. Classical theories are not expected to hold under these conditions. Some theories, such as loop quantum gravity, suggest singularities may not exist, and it is unknown whether they truly exist in real black holes.

Wave of [[Spacetime|spacetime]] curvature produced by the relative motion of gravitating masses, propagating at the speed of light. [[Albert Einstein]] first predicted them as a consequence of his [[General relativity|general theory of relativity]]. Hundreds have since been observed, first indirectly through [[Pulsar|binary-pulsar]] observations and, since 2015, directly by dedicated observatories. Newtonian gravity, by contrast, has no such waves, because it treats gravity as acting instantaneously everywhere. Unlike electromagnetic radiation, gravitational waves are not affected by intervening matter, so they can reveal [[Binary star|binary star]] systems, [[Supernova|supernovae]] and the early universe. The first direct detection came in September 2015, when detectors received a signal from the merger of two [[Black hole|black holes]]. Gravitational waves carry energy as gravitational radiation.

Hypothetical [[Elementary particle|elementary particle]] that mediates the gravitational interaction. If it exists, the graviton would be a massless [[Boson|spin-2 boson]], because gravitation's source is the [[Tensor|stress–energy tensor]]. Any massless spin-2 field would produce a force indistinguishable from gravity. No complete quantum field theory of gravitons exists, because renormalization in [[General relativity|general relativity]] remains unsolved. [[String theory]] avoids the problem by treating the graviton as a massless state of a fundamental string. The term was coined in 1934 by Soviet physicists Dmitry Blokhintsev and Fyodor Galperin. No graviton has been detected.

Spaceflight flyby that uses the gravity of a planet or other [[Astronomical object|astronomical object]] to alter a spacecraft's path and speed. Typically used to save propellant and reduce expense, the maneuver can accelerate or decelerate a spacecraft or redirect it. The first use came in 1959, when the Soviet probe Luna 3 photographed the far side of Earth's Moon. Interplanetary probes have used it from Mariner 10 onward, and the two Voyager probes made notable flybys of [[Jupiter]] and [[Saturn]]. [[Momentum]] gained by the spacecraft is matched by a loss to the body, in line with Newton's Third Law, but for a planet the change in speed is negligibly small. By minimizing reliance on chemical rockets, gravity assists have made ambitious deep-space missions feasible.

Net acceleration imparted to objects by the combined effect of gravitation and the centrifugal force from [[Earth's rotation]]. Near the surface it is about 9.8 m/s², so a freely falling object gains about 9.8 metres per second in speed every second, ignoring air resistance. Its strength varies by around 0.7% across Earth's surface, from 9.7639 m/s² on the Nevado Huascarán mountain in Peru to 9.8337 m/s² at the [[Arctic Ocean]]. The standard value of 9.80665 m/s² was defined in 1901 by the third General Conference on Weights and Measures.

SI unit (symbol Gy) of [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]] dose, equal to the absorption of one [[Joule|joule]] of radiation energy per [[Kilogram|kilogram]] of matter. It measures the energy deposited in a unit mass of absorbing material and is used to measure delivered doses in [[Radiation therapy|radiotherapy]], food irradiation and radiation sterilization. The gray is important in predicting likely acute health effects, such as [[Acute radiation syndrome]], and is used with the [[Sievert|sievert]] to calculate equivalent dose. Adopted into the [[International System of Units]] in 1975, it is named after British physicist Louis Harold Gray, a pioneer in measuring X-ray and radium radiation. The older cgs unit, the rad, equals 0.01 Gy and remains common largely in the United States.

Method of [[Animal husbandry|animal husbandry]] in which domestic [[Livestock|livestock]] range outdoors and consume wild vegetation. Grazing converts the cellulose in grass and other forage into meat, milk, wool and other animal products, often on land unsuitable for arable farming. Grazing livestock has been practiced since the beginning of agriculture, when [[Sheep]] and goats were domesticated by [[Nomad|nomads]] before permanent settlements around 7000 BC. In the [[Eurasian Steppe]], herds of sheep and horses were the primary means of food production for horseback nomads of Inner Asia. Ranching is the more common method today, sometimes supplemented with [[Hay|hay]] and fodder. Livestock grazing contributes to deforestation, extinction of native wildlife, soil degradation and desertification. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization, grazing systems cover about 60% of the world's grassland.

1978 American musical romantic comedy film directed by Randal Kleiser. Based on the 1971 stage musical by Jim Jacobs and Warren Casey, *Grease* stars [[John Travolta]] and [[Olivia Newton-John]] as Danny Zuko and Sandy Olsson. Released by [[Paramount Pictures]] on June 16, 1978, it was the highest-grossing film of 1978 and the highest-grossing musical film at the time. Its soundtrack ended 1978 as the second-best-selling album in the United States. "Hopelessly Devoted to You" was nominated for an Academy Award. In 2020 it was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry by the [[Library of Congress]].

Largest and deepest artesian basin in the world, underlying 22% of the [[Australia (continent)|Australian continent]]. It covers about 1,700,000 square kilometres and is estimated to hold 64,900 cubic kilometres of [[Groundwater|groundwater]]. Most recharge enters along the eastern edge, in [[Queensland]] and [[New South Wales]], and flows slowly toward the south and west through sandstone laid down during the Triassic, Jurassic and early Cretaceous periods. Before European settlement, its water discharged through mound springs. Boreholes now tap the pressurized water for stock, [[Irrigation|irrigation]] and domestic use, often without pumps. Because recharge is much less than extraction, water use from the basin is effectively a mining operation. The Great Artesian Basin Coordinating Committee coordinates activity among federal, state, territory and local governments.

Region of enhanced gravitational attraction in the local universe, approximately 150–250 million [[Light-year|light-years]] from the [[Milky Way]]. Its presence was inferred from peculiar motions of galaxies that deviate from the motion expected solely from the expansion of the universe. It is not a single galaxy or cluster but a broad concentration of matter. Early models attributed to it a mass of about 10¹⁶ [[Solar mass|solar masses]]. Later observations showed that nearby galaxies cannot be explained by this region alone, and that the more distant Shapley Supercluster contributes substantially. Lying behind the Milky Way's plane in the Zone of Avoidance, it is studied through X-ray, radio, infrared and neutral-hydrogen observations. It was incorporated into the definition of the [[Laniakea Supercluster]] in 2014.

Large oceanic bight (open gulf) off the southern coast of mainland [[Australia]]. Two definitions of its extent are used, by the International Hydrographic Organization and by the Australian Hydrographic Service, which places it in the [[Southern Ocean]]; it is generally considered part of the [[Indian Ocean]]. Its coastline is marked by cliffs and rocky capes, making it an ideal location for whale-watching. European explorers first encountered it in 1627, and English navigator Matthew Flinders charted it accurately in 1802. The bight came into existence about 50 million years ago, when the supercontinent [[Gondwana]] broke apart and separated [[Antarctica]] from Australia. Its waters are highly biodiverse, especially in zooplankton. Attempts to explore for oil and gas since the 1960s have faced significant opposition because of potential environmental impacts.

World's largest [[Coral reef|coral reef]] system, off the coast of [[Queensland]], Australia. It is composed of more than 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands, stretching over 2,300 kilometres across an area of about 344,400 square kilometres in the [[Coral Sea]]. Built by billions of coral polyps, it can be seen from [[Outer space|outer space]] and is the world's biggest structure made by living organisms. It has been a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site since 1981, and [[CNN]] named it one of the Seven Natural Wonders of the World in 1997. Pressures include [[Climate change|climate change]], accompanied by mass coral bleaching, and outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish. A study published in October 2012 found that the reef had lost more than half its coral cover since 1985. A 2022 survey reported the greatest recovery in 36 years, mainly through regrowth of two-thirds of the reef by fast-growing Acropora coral.

Largest lake entirely within Canada, in the [[Northwest Territories]] on the [[Arctic Circle]]. It is the fourth-largest lake in North America, with a surface area of 31,153 km² and a maximum depth of 446 m. It drains through the Great Bear River into the [[Mackenzie River]]. The lake is known for its clarity: explorer John Franklin wrote in 1828 that a white rag placed in the water did not disappear until it exceeded a depth of 15 fathoms. It lies between the Kazan Uplands of the [[Canadian Shield]] and the Interior Plains. In 1930 Gilbert LaBine discovered [[Uranium|uranium]] deposits in the region, and the Port Radium site on the eastern shore was later worked for silver and copper. The lake is covered with ice from late November to July.

Famine that struck [[Bengal]] and [[Bihar]] between 1769 and 1770, affecting some 30 million people, about one third of the area's population. It occurred under dual governance: the [[East India Company]] held the right to collect revenue, while civil administration remained with the Mughal governor, the Nawab of Bengal. Crop failures in autumn 1768 and summer 1769 and a [[Smallpox|smallpox]] epidemic preceded it. Grain merchants stopped advancing grain to [[Peasant|peasants]], and the Company bought large quantities of rice for its army. Rice prices rose two-fold by the end of 1769 and a further three-fold in 1770. Contemporary estimates put deaths at between seven and ten million, but some scholars consider these exaggerated and estimate at least 1 million. The famine hastened the end of dual governance, with the Company becoming sole administrator soon after.

Island in the [[Atlantic Ocean|North Atlantic]] off the northwest coast of continental [[Europe]], comprising England, Scotland and Wales. It is the largest of the [[British Isles]], the largest European island and the ninth-largest island in the world, with an area of 209,331 km². It has a maritime climate with narrow temperature differences between seasons. Connected to mainland Europe until 9,000 years ago by a land bridge now known as Doggerland, it has been inhabited by modern humans for around 30,000 years. In 2011 it had a population of about 61 million, making it the world's third-most-populous island after [[Java]] in Indonesia and [[Honshu]] in Japan. The term Great Britain can also refer to the political territory of England, Scotland and Wales, which with Northern Ireland forms the [[United Kingdom]].

Famine in the [[China|People's Republic of China]] from 1959 to 1961, widely regarded as the deadliest famine in history. Death estimates range from 15 to 46 million, with newer estimates concentrated around 30 to 46 million. The most stricken provinces included Anhui (18% dead). Causes included the policies of the [[Great Leap Forward]] and people's communes, high state grain confiscation, and over-reporting of food production. In 1962 Liu Shaoqi attributed 30% of the famine to natural disasters and 70% to man-made errors. In 1981 the [[Chinese Communist Party]] attributed it mainly to Great Leap Forward mistakes.

Cordillera system in eastern [[Australia]], the longest mountain chain entirely within a single country. It stretches more than 3,500 kilometres from Dauan Island in the Torres Strait, running along the east coast through [[Queensland]] and [[New South Wales]] before turning west across [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]]. Its width varies from about 160 to over 300 km. It is mainland Australia's most substantial topographic feature and the definitive watershed for eastern river systems, hence its name. Rivers east of the range drain into the [[Pacific Ocean]] and the [[Tasman Sea]], while rivers to the west drain in various westerly directions. The highest point is [[Mount Kosciuszko]], at 2,228 m in the Snowy Mountains. The range consists of limestones, sandstones and schists shaped by faulting and folding.

Bildungsroman by [[Charles Dickens]], serialised weekly in *All the Year Round* from December 1, 1860, to August 1861. The thirteenth novel by Dickens, *Great Expectations* follows an orphan, Pip, and is narrated in the first person. Set in [[Kent]] and London in the early to mid-19th century, it features the eccentric Miss Havisham, the cold Estella and the kindly blacksmith Joe Gargery. Thomas Carlyle disparaged it as "that Pip nonsense", but George Bernard Shaw praised it as "all of one piece and consistently truthful". In 2003 it ranked 17th in the [[BBC]] Big Read poll.

Period of mass starvation and disease in [[Ireland]] from 1845 to 1852. Its proximate cause was blight that infected [[Potato|potato]] crops across Europe, but longer-term factors included absentee landlordism and dependence on a single crop. Excess deaths are estimated at 775,000 to 1.5 million, and related mass emigration was one million or more. The worst year was 1847, known as "Black '47". A new Whig administration in London, pursuing [[Laissez-faire|laissez-faire]] policy, ended initial government relief measures. Large quantities of food continued to be exported from Ireland, a controversy that contributed to the intensification of Irish nationalism and anti-British sentiment. The population fell by 20–25% between 1841 and 1871, and the famine became part of Irish folk memory.

Hypothesized barrier that interrupts development from [[Abiogenesis|abiogenesis]] to advanced [[Civilization|civilizations]]. Economist Robin Hanson's name for a staple of Cold War discussion: if humans could send bacteria across the galaxy, why has no other species done so? Hanson laid out the chain of steps needed for such futures and asked which were most implausible. The argument implies that the more probable it is for life to reach humanity's stage, the bleaker humanity's future chances probably are. The idea is linked to the [[Fermi paradox]].

Fire that gutted the medieval [[City of London]] from September 2 to 5, 1666. It started shortly after midnight in a bakery on Pudding Lane, and wind fanned it into a firestorm that defeated efforts to create firebreaks by demolition. Order broke down as rumours of suspicious foreigners setting fires spread, and the French and Dutch communities, England's enemies in the Second Anglo-Dutch War, suffered street violence. On Tuesday the fire spread over nearly the whole city, destroying Old St Paul's Cathedral. It was halted when the wind dropped and the garrison of the [[Tower of London]] used [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] to create firebreaks. The death toll is generally thought to have been relatively small, though some historians challenge this. London was rebuilt on essentially the same medieval street plan.
